The eleven-year business trip of Hovhannes Joughayetsi, an Armenian merchant from New Julfa, the Armenian suburb of Isfahan in Safavid Iran, from 1682 to 1693. His surviving account book is one of the most detailed records of early modern long-distance trade.

He travelled south to the Persian Gulf, by sea to Surat in Mughal India, across north India, and over the Himalaya through Nepal to Lhasa in Tibet, where he stayed several years. He dealt in silver, gold, cloth, musk and other goods.

He was not trading with his own money. He was an agent working for wealthy merchants back in New Julfa under a contract that shared the profits between them. At each stop he found Armenian partners, credit and letters that linked him to a network stretching from Amsterdam and Venice to Manila. Courts and church in New Julfa enforced the deals. The network went back to the deportation of Armenians to Isfahan by Shah Abbas in 1604 and rivalled the great European trading companies such as the Dutch East India Company.
